title: Pelican Biosciences — oncall triage & integration scratchpad
content:
Quick context:
- Customer: Pelican Biosciences (clinical diagnostics, US, HIPAA scope). Using Redwood Private in their GCP-VPC with on-prem data connectors. They requested 99.9% latency SLO for inference tail p95 < 250ms for short prompts (<=128 tokens).
- Primary contact: Dr. Anil Rao (CTO) + SRE lead: Jorge Velasquez (not in Redwood contacts yet).
- Primary model: trimmed-medqa-v2 (40B variant) running on 2x A100s with quantized profile q4_0.

Call notes (2026-01-22 customer kick-off + 2026-02-18 follow-up incident):
- 01/22: walked through architecture: private control plane, customer-managed VPC peering, and edge gateway. They plan to route PHI through a dedicated subnet with KMS-managed keys.
- 02/18 incident: periodic spikes where tails blow past 1s for 3–5 minute windows. Customer called — high priority.
  - Observed behavior: CPU usage on proxy hosts spiked; GPU utilization uneven (one card 95%, other idle); request queue grew at runtime layer.
  - They use a synchronous request pattern from their app (no streaming) with 3 replicas behind our edge proxy per model.
  - Burst pattern: sudden batch of ~45 concurrent short requests (prompt len < 100) from their nightly ingest agent.

Immediate triage steps taken (by oncall):
- Checked route: requests were being routed to single replica due to misconfigured sticky-session rule on their app LB. Confirmed via edge-proxy logs: x-forwarded-for and session cookie mapped to replica-1.
- Scaled replicas manually to 5 to absorb burst.
- Flushed prefix cache on replica-1 to remove stale KV fragments (had been growing suspiciously; suspect underlying integration loop).
- Applied temporary rate-limit on ingest agent (client-side) to smooth bursts.

Root-cause hypotheses & evidence:
1) LB sticky sessions + single-replica routing
   - Evidence: edge logs show same client IP -> same backend ID during spikes.
   - Action: ask customer infra to remove sticky-cookie or enable round-robin at LB.
2) KV cache fragmentation and memory leak in their prompt preprocessor creating large prefix keys
   - Evidence: replica-1 mem growth before GPU spike; cache hit ratio dropping.
   - Action: recommend prefix eviction policy and reconfigure cache TTL to 5m for short prompt workloads.
3) Model scheduling / kernel hotpath misbalance between cards
   - Evidence: one card hot, other idle. Could be GPU-affinity / device assignment on their node pool or container pinned incorrectly.
   - Action: capture nvtop and nvidia-smi while reproducing; check container runtime flags --gpus and CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES mapping.

Short-term mitigations applied to keep customer stable:
- Increased replica count to 5 (manual) and pinned a load-distribution policy to round-robin in our routing layer.
- Enabled request shaping: max concurrency per-replica = 8 for short-prompts route.
- Temporary 90s batching window disabled (they had opted-in previously) — batching caused queue-to-gpu longer tails during bursts.

Config recommendations (next planned work):
- LB: remove sticky session cookie for inference endpoints; use consistent-hash only for long-conversation routes.
- Cache: set prefix cache TTL = 300s, limit per-session prefix fragments = 12. Add cache-size watermark at 70% to trigger eviction.
- Runtime: enforce balanced device assignment in nodepool (round-robin CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES), add health-check that fails-over replicas if GPU-imbalance > 40% for 30s.
- Autoscale: set policy to scale by replica on p95 CPU or queue length threshold rather than GPU util. For short prompt workloads p95 queue-length > 25 -> +1 replica, cooldown 45s.

Operational playbook (for oncall):
- First 5 minutes: check edge-proxy logs and replica routing (grep for backend-id), look for repeated X-Forwarded-For and session-cookie correlations.
- Next 10 minutes: check per-node GPU utilization (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv), container-level cgroups for affinity issues.
- If single-replica hot: scale replicas and enable round-robin routing; verify cache pressure.
- If queue length grows > 60s: disable batching and inform customer to throttle bulk agents.

Commands / quick runbook snippets (oncall):
- tail -n 200 /var/log/edge-proxy/request.log | grep "pelican-bio" | jq '.backend_id, .client_ip'
- kubectl top pod -n private-deploy | sort -k3 -nr
- ssh node-A sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,utilization.gpu,memory.total,memory.used --format=csv
- curl -X POST https://private-controlplane/api/v1/route/update -d '{"service":"pelican-bio","policy":"round-robin"}'  # ops only

Outstanding tasks / next steps (owners & ETA):
- (Maya) Draft runbook for Pelican (this doc -> cleaned) and share with SRE; ETA 2026-03-05.
- (Ethan) Add automatic detection alert for sticky-session routing pattern to routing monitoring (PROJ-4532); ETA 2026-03-10.
- (Sofia) Prototype prefix cache TTL autosuggest in Redwood Optimize for short prompt workloads; ETA 2026-03-18.
- (Customer) Pelican infra: remove LB sticky cookie or enable consistent-hash only for conversations; (customer action) ETA their side: 2026-03-03.

Open questions / unresolved:
- Why did the prefix cache grow only on replica-1? Is it client behavior (same prefix keys to one replica) or a backend loop? Need profiler traces of preprocessor (customer to share).
- Can we safely recommend disabling batching for all short-prompt health-critical routes? Cost implications — need to model token cost vs latency improvements.
- Does their KMS integration add extra latency to mesh at scale (per-request key unwrap)? Our initial profiling didn't show big hits but need to run under load.

Notes to self (todo during follow-up call):
- Request small synthetic load from customer that mimics the ingest agent: 40 concurrent, 50ms inter-arrival, prompts 60–90 tokens. Keep monitoring logs.
- Get access to one of their LB configs (screenshot) and the cloud route table to verify session persistence settings.
- Ask Jorge for their node pool autoscaling policy and GPU assignment script (if any).

Risks & impact summary (for escalation):
- If sticky sessions persist + ingest bursts, risk of a single replica meltdown -> 99.9 SLO breach and potential data-plane timeouts.
- KV cache leak can cause OOM and long cold-start times for replicas.
- KMS per-request latency could amplify tail if combined with queueing.

Back-of-envelope cost note (for discussion with customer):
- Disabling batching increases per-token GPU cycles ~ +12% in our internal tests for short prompts, but reduces tail latency by ~40–60ms in burst scenarios. For their 2k qps baseline this could mean ~+$1.2k/mo; estimate rough, needs formal calc.

End-of-notes.

(keep this informal — will convert to proper runbook once we confirm root cause and customer LB change)
